In case that wasn't a rhetorical question, it all comes down to a law called Title IX which says that:

No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving federal financial assistance.

It seems on the surface to be a very inoffensive and egalitarian proposal. After all, why would anyone want sex based discrimination? However, it's actually extraordinarily dangerous because it effectively gives the department of education the power to determine campus policy in pretty much any area with absolute compliance on pain of loss of federal funding.

One extension of this was the "Dear Colleague letter" written several years ago which advised colleges that permitting a student who had sexually assaulted another student to continue attending campus was a form of latent harassment and a breach of title IX. As such, colleges were required to set up tribunals to determine the truth of any such claims and, if they found the preponderence of evidence ("more likely than not," not "beyond all reasonable doubt") to fall in favour of the accuser, the accused is to be ejected from campus, with a note as to the reason on their transcript.

In practice, this determination is carried out by women's studies professors, so you can imagine the kind of bias involved. Also, the accuser is automatically assigned counsel, but the accused is not permitted to bring anyone with them to the hearing as they feel that having lawyers involved would diminish the educational experience and that being tried in such a manner is an educational opportunity for male students. They're also forbidden to cross examine their accuser and usually aren't given access to the details of the accusation in advance.
